title: Naming Coordination Compounds
short: Name the ligands in alphabetical order with prefixes, then the metal and its oxidation state.
trouble: Students alphabetize ligands by their number prefixes, or forget the -ate ending for a metal in a complex anion.

blocks.html: Once you can find the parts of a coordination compound, its name follows a fixed recipe. The name tells a chemist every ligand, the metal and its oxidation state.

Name the cation first, then the anion, as for any salt. Inside the complex: ligands in alphabetical order (ignoring number prefixes), each with a prefix for how many (di-, tri-, tetra-; or bis-, tris- for ligands like ethylenediamine), then the metal with its oxidation state in Roman numerals. If the complex is an anion, the metal takes the ending -ate.

The rules make every name unique and reversible: from the name you can write the formula, and back. Anionic ligands end in -o (current IUPAC names end in -ido: chlorido, cyanido; older books use chloro, cyano). Neutral ligands have special names: ammine ($\mathrm{NH_3}$), aqua ($\mathrm{H_2O}$), carbonyl (CO). The -ate ending signals a negative complex, just as sulfate and nitrate are anions. Some -ate names use the Latin root: ferrate (Fe), cuprate (Cu), argentate (Ag), plumbate (Pb), aurate (Au), stannate (Sn).

blocks.title: A complex cation
steps: Complex cation $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^+}$; anion chloride. Cobalt: $x + 0 + 2(-1) = +1$, so Co(III).
Ligands alphabetically: ammine (a) before chlorido (c): tetraammine, dichlorido.

blocks.title: A complex anion
steps: Cation: potassium. Complex anion $\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}$: $x + 6(-1) = -3$, so Fe(III).
Six cyanido ligands: hexacyanido. Anion, so iron becomes ferrate.

blocks.title: From name to formula
blocks.q: Write the formula of diamminesilver(I) nitrate.

blocks.html: Formulas follow their own order: inside the brackets, the metal comes first, then the ligands. Many books list neutral ligands before anionic ones, as in $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^+}$; current IUPAC rules list ligands alphabetically by their formulas. Either way, the brackets enclose the complex and its charge sits outside them.

Alphabetizing ligands by their number prefixes, which would put "dichlorido" before "tetraammine" because d comes before t. Prefixes are ignored: compare "chlorido" with "ammine." Also, forgetting the -ate ending for a metal in a complex anion. Check: if the brackets carry a negative charge, the metal's name must end in -ate.
